stem: A 52-year-old woman with known gallstones has sudden severe upper abdominal pain going through to her back, with vomiting. She leans forward to ease it. Serum lipase is 8 times normal, and CT shows fluid around a swollen pancreas. She drinks no alcohol and her triglycerides and calcium are normal.
oneliner: 52F + gallstones + sudden epigastric pain to back, eased leaning forward + lipase ×8 + peripancreatic fluid + no alcohol, normal TG and Ca → what started it?
ask: Obstruction at which site most likely started this?

whyNot.A: Cystic duct stone gives **acute cholecystitis** (RUQ pain, Murphy sign), not a raised lipase
whyNot.C: Blocks bile above the cystic duct junction: **jaundice**, but the pancreatic duct drains below it
whyNot.D: **Mesenteric ischemia**: pain out of proportion to exam; lipase not the clue
whyNot.E: Lymph channel: blockage gives **chylous ascites**, not pancreatitis

answer: Gallstone blocking the ampulla of Vater
why: A stone lodged at the **ampulla** blocks the **shared exit of bile and pancreatic ducts**. Pancreatic juice backs up, **trypsin is activated inside the gland**, and the pancreas digests itself.

idea.rule: Pancreatitis = enzymes switched on inside the pancreas instead of in the gut.
also: Alcohol (sphincter spasm, protein plugs)
Hypertriglyceridemia (>1,000 mg/dL)
Hypercalcemia (calcium activates trypsinogen)
ERCP, scorpion sting, mumps

stem: A 61-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis vomits blood, then becomes drowsy and confused over a day. He is jaundiced, has ascites and dilated veins around the umbilicus, and shows a flapping tremor when he extends his wrists. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, oxygen saturation is 97% on room air, and hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL.
oneliner: 61M + cirrhosis + hematemesis → drowsy, confused + jaundice, ascites, periumbilical veins + flapping tremor + BP 118/72, SpO2 97%, Hb 10.1 → mechanism of confusion?
ask: Which mechanism best explains his confusion?

options.D: Gut-derived nitrogenous toxins, mainly ammonia, bypassing a failing liver

whyNot.A: His **saturation is 97%**
whyNot.B: His **blood pressure is normal**
whyNot.C: **Budd-Chiari** gives acute pain and tender hepatomegaly; nothing here points to it, and his confusion follows the **bleed**
whyNot.E: Hb 10.1 reduces oxygen content but **does not cause asterixis**

answer: Hyperammonemia from blood in the gut and portosystemic shunting
why: **Digested blood is a protein load**; bacteria convert it to **ammonia**. A cirrhotic liver with **portosystemic shunts** cannot clear it, so ammonia reaches the brain, where **astrocytes make glutamine and swell**. **Asterixis** is the classic sign.
chain: GI bleed adds protein to the gut
Failed liver and shunts, so it is not cleared

idea.rule: In cirrhosis, a GI bleed, infection, or constipation can push gut ammonia high enough to cause encephalopathy.
also: Treat with lactulose and rifaximin
Other triggers: infection, constipation, diuretics, TIPS
Protein restriction is not advised long term

stem: A 45-year-old woman has burning behind the breastbone after large fatty meals, relieved only briefly by antacids. She has no trouble swallowing. Esophageal manometry shows normal resting lower esophageal sphincter pressure and normal peristalsis, but pH monitoring shows acid exposure that begins soon after eating, in short episodes.
oneliner: 45F + burning after large fatty meals + antacids only briefly help + no dysphagia + manometry: normal resting LES pressure, normal peristalsis + acid episodes soon after eating → mechanism of reflux?
ask: Which mechanism most likely allows the reflux?

options.A: Gastrin-induced relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter
options.B: Vagally mediated transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter
options.C: Failure of the sphincter to relax on swallowing
options.D: A permanently low resting sphincter pressure

whyNot.A: **Gastrin raises** sphincter tone
whyNot.C: **Achalasia**: dysphagia, high resting pressure
whyNot.D: Her **resting pressure is normal**
whyNot.E: Her **peristalsis is normal** on manometry

answer: Transient LES relaxations triggered by gastric distension
why: After a **large meal the stomach distends**, and a **vagal reflex** briefly **relaxes the LES** without swallowing. **Acid refluxes in short episodes** soon after eating. **Fat slows gastric emptying and lowers LES tone** (CCK), worsening it.

idea.rule: Most GERD is from transient LES relaxations, not a permanently weak sphincter.
also: Hiatal hernia, obesity, pregnancy and smoking lower LES tone
Chronic reflux can cause Barrett esophagus
Fat, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol relax the LES

stem: A 47-year-old man has had 6 months of burning epigastric pain and watery, greasy diarrhea. Endoscopy shows ulcers in the duodenum and the proximal jejunum, and they recur after each course of proton pump inhibitor. Tests for Helicobacter pylori are negative and he takes no NSAIDs.
oneliner: 47M + epigastric pain + diarrhea + ulcers in duodenum and jejunum + recurrence on PPI + H pylori negative, no NSAIDs → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains his ulcers?

options.D: Blunted villi from an immune reaction to gluten

whyNot.A: **H pylori** is negative
whyNot.B: **NSAIDs** cause this and he takes none
whyNot.D: **Celiac** gives diarrhea but not recurrent ulcers
whyNot.E: Causes **gastritis** in the stomach, not jejunal ulcers

answer: Gastrinoma drives uncontrolled acid secretion
why: A **gastrin-secreting tumor** (gastrinoma) overstimulates parietal cells, producing **massive acid output**. Ulcers appear in unusual places like the **jejunum** and the **acid inactivates pancreatic lipase**, giving steatorrhea.

idea.rule: Ulcers in unusual locations or refractory to PPIs suggest Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
also: Diagnose with elevated fasting gastrin and a secretin stimulation test
Part of MEN1 in some patients
Tumors usually in the 'gastrinoma triangle' (duodenum and pancreas)

stem: A 49-year-old woman has had 2 months of nausea and a 6-kg weight loss, and now bruises easily. Prothrombin time is prolonged, the aPTT is mildly prolonged, and the platelet count is normal. ALT is 640 U/L. She takes no anticoagulants.
oneliner: 49F + nausea, weight loss + easy bruising + prolonged PT, mild aPTT prolongation + normal platelets + ALT 640 → which cell's failure causes the coagulopathy?
ask: Damage to which of the following cell types most likely explains the prolonged prothrombin time?

whyNot.A: They make **vWF and tPA**; their injury doesn't prolong the PT
whyNot.B: Lay down **collagen**; they do not produce clotting factors
whyNot.D: **Kupffer cells** clear antigens but do not synthesize factors
whyNot.E: Mediate **immune** responses; they have no role in factor synthesis

answer: Injured hepatocytes make fewer clotting factors
why: **Hepatocytes** make most clotting factors (**I, II, V, VII, IX, X, XI**) and proteins C and S. With **hepatocellular injury** (ALT 640), synthesis falls and the **PT rises first** because factor VII has the shortest half-life.
chain: Factor VII falls first, PT rises

idea.rule: The liver makes most clotting factors; PT rises early in liver failure and does not correct with vitamin K.
also: Vitamin K deficiency also prolongs PT but corrects with vitamin K
Factor VIII is made by endothelium, so it is spared in liver disease
INR is part of the MELD score

stem: A 55-year-old man with 25 years of heavy alcohol use has spider angiomata, ascites and a firm liver edge. He vomits a large volume of bright red blood without preceding retching, and his blood pressure falls.
oneliner: 55M + 25 y alcohol + spider angiomata + ascites + hematemesis, no preceding retching + hypotension → why bleeding vessels in the esophagus?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the source of bleeding?

options.A: Erosion of an aortic aneurysm into the esophagus
options.B: Diversion of portal blood into dilated submucosal esophageal veins
options.C: Acid injury of the lower esophagus
options.D: Opening of arteriovenous shunts in the mesentery
options.E: Mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction

whyNot.A: Would present with a **herald bleed** and chest pain, and has no link to liver disease
whyNot.C: Reflux esophagitis causes **heartburn and ulcers**, rarely massive bleeding
whyNot.D: Would not produce **bleeding veins in the esophagus**
whyNot.E: Needs **forceful retching**, which he did not have

answer: Esophageal varices from portosystemic collaterals
why: Cirrhosis raises **portal pressure**. Blood is diverted from the **left gastric vein** into **esophageal submucosal veins**, which drain to the **azygos** system. These **thin-walled veins dilate and rupture**.
chain: Portal blood diverted via left gastric vein

idea.rule: Portal hypertension opens portosystemic anastomoses; the esophagus is one of them.
also: Umbilical (paraumbilical) veins: caput medusae
Rectal veins: hemorrhoids
Retroperitoneal veins

stem: A 72-year-old man dies of a stroke. At autopsy, a segment of his sigmoid colon is opened and shown. The muscular wall between the outpouchings appears thickened.
oneliner: 72M + autopsy + sigmoid colon with outpouchings in rows → how did these form?
ask: Which of the following best explains the formation of these outpouchings?

options.B: Raised intraluminal pressure pushing mucosa and submucosa through weak points in the wall
options.E: Ischemic necrosis of the bowel wall

whyNot.A: The wall between pouches is **thickened**, not atrophic
whyNot.C: The sacs are **smooth pouches**; no mass or irregular lesion
whyNot.D: A **congenital** (true) diverticulum includes all wall layers and is usually solitary (Meckel)
whyNot.E: Ischemia gives **hemorrhagic, dusky** mucosa, not discrete sacs

answer: Mucosal and submucosal herniation through weak points in the muscularis (pseudodiverticula)
why: A low-fiber diet and **raised colonic pressure** push mucosa and submucosa out where **vasa recta pierce the muscularis**, between the taeniae coli. These **false diverticula** lack muscularis and are most common in the **sigmoid**.
chain: Low fiber, hard stool, high pressure

idea.rule: Pulsion diverticula: high pressure pushes mucosa through weak spots in the muscle wall, giving false diverticula.
also: Sigmoid diverticulosis: highest colonic pressure, weak points at vasa recta
Zenker diverticulum: above the cricopharyngeus (Killian triangle)
Bladder diverticula from outlet obstruction (BPH)
Contrast: Meckel is a true, congenital diverticulum

image.prompt: Gross photograph of an opened segment of sigmoid colon showing multiple small, round mucosal openings of outpouchings arranged in rows along the colon wall, with thickened muscular wall between them. Neutral background. No text or labels.

stem: A 54-year-old man has had 6 months of bulky, foul, oily stools that float and leave a greasy ring in the toilet, with an 8-kg weight loss. He has drunk heavily for 25 years and has had several earlier bouts of upper abdominal pain. He has had no bowel surgery and no blood in the stool. An abdominal x-ray is shown.
oneliner: 54M + heavy alcohol 25 y + bulky oily floating stools + 8 kg weight loss + past epigastric pain + no bowel surgery + abdominal x-ray → mechanism of the stools?
ask: Which of the following best explains his stools?

options.A: Rapid intestinal transit from a motility disorder
options.C: Loss of ileal bile acid reabsorption

whyNot.A: Transit disorders cause **watery**, not greasy, stools; nothing here suggests it
whyNot.B: Gives **watery** diarrhea that stops with fasting, not oily floating stools
whyNot.C: Needs **ileal disease or resection**; he has had no bowel surgery
whyNot.E: Causes **varices and ascites**; not oily stools

answer: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (chronic pancreatitis with steatorrhea)
why: **Alcohol, repeated pain and the calcified pancreas on x-ray** point to chronic pancreatitis. Lipase is lost first and most completely, so fat is not digested, and **fatty (oily) stools with weight loss** follow.
chain: Years of alcohol injure the pancreas
Acinar tissue is replaced by fibrosis and calcium
Lipase and other enzymes fall below about 10% of normal

idea.rule: Oily, floating stools with pancreatic calcification mean lost pancreatic enzyme output.
also: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are malabsorbed
Late complication: diabetes from islet loss
Treatment: pancreatic enzyme capsules with meals
Other causes: cystic fibrosis, pancreatic duct obstruction

image.prompt: Plain frontal abdominal radiograph of an adult showing multiple small, coarse, speckled calcifications scattered across the upper abdomen in the line of the pancreas, crossing the spine at the L1-L2 level. Normal bowel gas pattern. No text, labels or arrows.

stem: A 58-year-old man with chronic alcohol use has foul, greasy stools and weight loss. Fecal fat is 24 g/day, fecal elastase is low, and a CT shows calcifications in the pancreas. A duodenal sample after a meal has a pH of 4.0. Bile acid levels are normal and a hydrogen breath test is normal.
oneliner: 58M + chronic alcohol + greasy foul stools + fecal fat 24 g/d + low fecal elastase + pancreatic calcification + duodenal pH 4.0 + normal bile acids and breath test → why fat is undigested?
ask: Which of the following best explains the poor fat digestion in his duodenum?

options.B: Loss of pancreatic bicarbonate, so lipase is inactivated in acidic contents
options.C: Reduced hepatic synthesis of bile acids
options.D: Premature activation of lipase inside the duct
options.E: Failure of ileal bile acid reabsorption

whyNot.A: A **normal hydrogen breath test** argues against overgrowth
whyNot.C: **Bile acid levels are normal**
whyNot.D: That is the mechanism of **acute** pancreatitis, not this chronic fibrosing picture
whyNot.E: Ileal disease would give **low bile acid pool**; his is normal

answer: Low duodenal pH from lost bicarbonate inactivates lipase
why: The damaged gland makes **less bicarbonate** as well as less enzyme. Gastric acid is then not neutralised, the **duodenal pH falls (below about 4.5)**, and **lipase is denatured** and bile salts precipitate, so fat digestion fails even more.
chain: Fibrosis destroys ductal and acinar cells
Lipase is inactivated and bile salts precipitate

idea.rule: Pancreatic insufficiency fails twice: fewer enzymes and a duodenum too acidic for the remaining enzymes to work.
also: Secretin from duodenal S cells drives ductal bicarbonate
Acid-suppressing drugs help enzyme replacement work
Low fecal elastase confirms exocrine failure
Cystic fibrosis causes the same by thick secretions

stem: A 61-year-old woman with childhood rheumatic fever has had palpitations and takes no blood thinner. She develops sudden severe periumbilical pain 3 hours ago with vomiting, but her abdomen is soft with little tenderness. Her pulse is irregularly irregular, and there is an apical diastolic rumble after an opening snap. Lactate is 5.2 mmol/L. She has never had pain after meals, has not lost weight, does not smoke and has normal cholesterol.
oneliner: 61F + old rheumatic fever + irregularly irregular pulse + diastolic rumble, opening snap + no anticoagulant + sudden severe periumbilical pain, soft abdomen + lactate 5.2 + no postprandial pain, normal lipids → mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best explains the bowel ischemia?

options.A: Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque at the artery origin
options.B: Embolus from the left atrium lodged in the superior mesenteric artery
options.E: Prolonged low-flow state in the mesenteric vessels

whyNot.A: No **vascular risk factors or prior postprandial pain**
whyNot.C: Usually follows **hypercoagulable states or portal hypertension** and has a slower course
whyNot.D: Would give **bloody stool and a falling hemoglobin**, not a sudden ischemic pain
whyNot.E: Needs **shock or heart failure**, and nothing suggests either

answer: Cardioembolic occlusion of the SMA in atrial fibrillation with mitral stenosis
why: **Mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation** stagnates blood in the left atrium and forms **thrombus**. A fragment travels to the **superior mesenteric artery**, causing sudden ischemia with **pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen**.
chain: Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium
Atrial fibrillation causes stasis and thrombus
Severe pain, lactate rise, later infarction

idea.rule: AF with mitral stenosis is the strongest setup for arterial emboli; the SMA is a common target.
also: Same left atrial clot: stroke, renal or splenic infarct, acute limb ischemia
Other cardiac sources: mural thrombus after MI, endocarditis vegetations
The SMA is a common target: wide, oblique take-off from the aorta
Anticoagulation in AF prevents these emboli

stem: A 3-day-old boy vomits green fluid after every feeding. His abdomen is flat except for fullness in the upper abdomen, and he has passed little stool. An upper gastrointestinal study shows a dilated stomach and proximal duodenum. At surgery, a band of pancreatic tissue encircles the second part of the duodenum.
oneliner: 3d M + bilious vomiting after every feed + upper abdominal fullness + dilated stomach and proximal duodenum + surgery: pancreatic tissue ring around D2 → which structure developed abnormally?
ask: Abnormal development of which structure most likely caused this obstruction?

whyNot.B: Forms the **body, tail and upper head**; it does not migrate around the duodenum
whyNot.C: Pyloric stenosis gives **non-bilious** vomiting and a palpable olive
whyNot.D: Remnant forms **Meckel diverticulum**, bleeding or intussusception, not high obstruction
whyNot.E: Causes **choking, cyanosis with feeds** and non-bilious vomiting

answer: Annular pancreas: ventral bud fails to rotate properly and encircles the duodenum
why: The **ventral bud** normally rotates behind the duodenum to fuse with the dorsal bud. If its tip **migrates in both directions around the duodenum**, a ring forms. Because the obstruction lies **below the ampulla**, the vomit is **bilious**.
chain: Ring of pancreatic tissue around D2
Bilious vomiting in the first days

idea.rule: Bilious vomiting in a newborn means obstruction beyond the ampulla until proven otherwise.
also: Duodenal atresia: double-bubble, Down syndrome
Annular pancreas often accompanies duodenal atresia
Malrotation with volvulus is a surgical emergency
Pyloric stenosis: non-bilious, 2 to 6 weeks old

stem: A 29-year-old woman has had 8 months of food sticking in her chest, from the start with both solid food and liquids. At night she regurgitates undigested food. She has lost 6 kg and does not have heartburn, and her skin and fingers are normal. A barium swallow is shown.
oneliner: 29F + 8 mo dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start + nocturnal regurgitation of undigested food + 6 kg weight loss + no heartburn, normal skin + barium swallow → underlying defect?
ask: Which of the following is the underlying defect?

options.A: Atrophy and fibrosis of esophageal smooth muscle
options.B: Acid injury causing a peptic stricture
options.D: Degeneration of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus

whyNot.A: Scleroderma gives a **weak, patulous sphincter with reflux**; she has no heartburn or skin changes
whyNot.B: Gives **solid-food dysphagia first and heartburn**, which she lacks
whyNot.C: A retching tear causes **bleeding after vomiting**, not months of dysphagia
whyNot.E: Zenker diverticulum sits in the **neck** of **older** adults; she is 29 and food sticks in her chest

answer: Achalasia: loss of myenteric inhibitory neurons (NO, VIP)
why: **Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start** suggests a motility disorder. Loss of **inhibitory neurons (nitric oxide, VIP)** leaves the **lower esophageal sphincter contracted** and removes peristalsis, giving a dilated esophagus with a **bird's-beak** narrowing.
chain: LES cannot relax and peristalsis is lost
Food and fluid stay in the esophagus

idea.rule: Dysphagia to solids and liquids together from the start means motility disorder; solids first means mechanical.
also: Chagas disease destroys the same neurons (Trypanosoma cruzi)
Manometry: high LES pressure, no relaxation
Increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma
Treatment: pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy, botulinum toxin

image.prompt: Barium esophagram, frontal view, showing a markedly dilated esophagus tapering smoothly to a narrow beak-like point at the gastroesophageal junction, with a retained column of barium and air-fluid level. No text, labels or arrows.

stem: A 4-year-old boy had influenza and was given aspirin for his fever. Five days later he has repeated vomiting and then becomes lethargic and has a seizure. The liver edge is 3 cm below the costal margin and he is not jaundiced. Blood glucose is 38 mg/dL, ammonia is markedly raised, and AST and ALT are 5 times normal. A liver biopsy photomicrograph is shown.
oneliner: 4M + flu + aspirin for fever + 5 d later vomiting, lethargy, seizure + hepatomegaly, no jaundice + glucose 38, ammonia high, AST/ALT ×5 + liver biopsy → which organelle is damaged?
ask: Dysfunction of which organelle is most responsible for these findings?

whyNot.B: Defects cause **I-cell disease** (failed lysosomal enzyme targeting), not hepatic failure with hyperammonemia
whyNot.C: Impairment causes **Kartagener syndrome and Chediak-Higashi**, with no ammonia rise
whyNot.D: Affects **protein synthesis**; does not explain fat accumulation with failed urea synthesis
whyNot.E: Defects cause **Zellweger syndrome** with very long chain fatty acid buildup, in infancy

answer: Reye syndrome: hepatic mitochondrial injury impairs fatty acid oxidation and the urea cycle
why: **Aspirin during viral illness in a child** leads to **hepatic mitochondrial damage**. **Beta-oxidation fails** (microvesicular fat, hypoglycemia) and **urea cycle enzymes in mitochondria fail** (hyperammonemia, encephalopathy and cerebral edema).
chain: Urea cycle fails (ornithine transcarbamylase, CPS I)

idea.rule: Reye syndrome: aspirin in a child with viral illness causes hepatic mitochondrial failure.
also: Avoid aspirin in children with influenza or varicella
No jaundice, high ammonia, microvesicular steatosis
Treatment is supportive: lower ICP, glucose
Fatty acid oxidation disorders look alike (MCAD deficiency)

image.prompt: High-power H&E photomicrograph of liver tissue showing hepatocytes with numerous tiny fat droplets filling the cytoplasm (microvesicular steatosis, foamy cytoplasm) with centrally placed round nuclei. No significant inflammation or necrosis. No text, labels or arrows.

stem: Healthy volunteers are given a citric acid candy or a placebo. With citric acid, saliva flow doubles compared with placebo. Saliva collected during citric acid stimulation has about twice the sodium and chloride concentration of the placebo sample, and is closer to plasma in its NaCl content.
oneliner: Volunteers + citric acid versus placebo + saliva flow ×2 + NaCl ×2 in stimulated saliva, closer to plasma → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains the higher NaCl in the fast-flow saliva?

options.A: Less time in the ducts for reabsorption of NaCl
options.B: Reduced water absorption by the ducts
options.D: Faster turnover of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the acini
options.E: Ducts that cannot take up chloride

whyNot.B: Ducts are **relatively water-impermeable** at all flow rates
whyNot.C: **Secretin** acts on the pancreas and bile ducts, not salivary glands
whyNot.D: Acinar fluid is **isotonic at any flow rate**; the difference arises later in the ducts
whyNot.E: Ducts **do reabsorb** Na and Cl, which is why placebo saliva is low in NaCl

answer: Ductal NaCl reabsorption falls when flow is fast
why: Acini secrete an **isotonic fluid**. **Ducts reabsorb Na+ and Cl- but not water**, making saliva hypotonic. At **high flow, contact time shortens**, so less NaCl is reabsorbed and saliva stays closer to plasma.
chain: Ducts reabsorb Na and Cl, not water

idea.rule: Faster flow = less ductal modification = saliva closer to plasma composition.
also: Slow flow: very hypotonic saliva, low Na and Cl
Sweat ducts behave the same: fast sweating gives saltier sweat
Renal analogy: fast tubular flow delivers more Na distally
Bicarbonate in saliva rises with flow

stem: A 4-week-old boy has vomited forcefully after every feed for 5 days. The vomit is milky and never green, and he feeds eagerly again afterward. He is below birth weight, and a firm olive-sized mass is felt in the right upper abdomen after a feed. Waves of peristalsis cross the upper abdomen.
oneliner: 4-week-old boy + projectile nonbilious vomiting + hungry after + weight loss + olive mass + visible peristalsis → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism most likely accounts for his vomiting?

options.C: Hypertrophy of the circular pyloric muscle narrowing the outlet
options.D: Failure of neural crest migration into the distal bowel
options.E: Midgut twisting around the superior mesenteric artery

whyNot.A: **Duodenal atresia**: bilious vomiting in the first days, double-bubble sign
whyNot.B: **Intussusception**: age 6 to 36 months, colicky pain, currant-jelly stool
whyNot.D: **Hirschsprung**: delayed meconium, distension and **bilious** vomiting; no olive mass
whyNot.E: **Volvulus**: **bilious** vomiting and an acute abdomen

answer: Pyloric muscle hypertrophy causing gastric outlet obstruction
why: Thickened **circular pyloric muscle** narrows the outlet, so feeds cannot leave the stomach. The vomit is **nonbilious** because it is **proximal to the ampulla**, and persistent loss of gastric acid causes **hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis**.

idea.rule: Nonbilious vomiting means the block is above the ampulla.
also: Gastric outlet obstruction from peptic ulcer scarring: nonbilious
Duodenal atresia (usually below the ampulla): bilious, double bubble
Malrotation with volvulus: bilious, a surgical emergency

stem: A 56-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis has fever and mild diffuse abdominal pain. He has ascites and no prior abdominal surgery or peritoneal dialysis catheter. He has no heart murmur, and imaging shows no free air and no liver abscess. Ascitic fluid has 1,100 leukocytes/mm3 with 80% neutrophils, low total protein and a single organism, E. coli, on culture.
oneliner: 56M + alcoholic cirrhosis + ascites + fever + ascitic WBC 1,100, 80% neutrophils + low protein + E. coli alone + no surgery, free air, abscess or murmur → how did it get in?
ask: What is the most likely route of infection?

options.A: Translocation of gut bacteria across the intestinal wall
options.C: Contiguous spread from a liver abscess
options.D: Direct inoculation through a dialysis catheter

whyNot.B: **Secondary peritonitis**: polymicrobial, free air, high protein; none here
whyNot.C: **Liver abscess** would be seen on imaging; **none is present**
whyNot.D: He has **no peritoneal catheter or recent procedure**
whyNot.E: **No murmur**, and a **single enteric organism** in cirrhotic ascites points to gut origin

answer: Gut flora cross the bowel wall into ascites that has poor opsonic activity
why: In cirrhosis, **portal hypertension and slow gut transit** let enteric bacteria **cross the intestinal wall**. Ascitic fluid with **low protein** has weak opsonic activity, so infection takes hold: **neutrophils above 250/mm3** with one organism defines **SBP**.
chain: Fever, abdominal pain, ascitic PMN over 250

idea.rule: Single enteric organism in ascites with cirrhosis = translocation, not perforation.
also: Secondary peritonitis: multiple organisms, high protein, low glucose
Prophylaxis after GI bleeding or prior SBP
Treat with cefotaxime plus albumin

stem: A 32-year-old woman has leaked stool for 14 months, since her first vaginal delivery, which needed forceps and had a third-degree perineal tear. She soils herself when she coughs or has a sudden urge. Anal squeeze is weak with a palpable gap anteriorly. Stool is formed, with no constipation or bleeding.
oneliner: 32F + leaks stool 14 mo since first forceps delivery with third-degree tear + weak squeeze, anterior gap + formed stool → which structure?
ask: Which structure was most likely damaged?

whyNot.A: Gives **bleeding or prolapse**, not loss of voluntary squeeze
whyNot.B: **Parasympathetic** supply of the distal colon and rectum; not the cause of a mechanical sphincter gap
whyNot.C: **Smooth muscle** for resting tone: loss gives passive leakage at rest, not a **weak voluntary squeeze**
whyNot.D: Mucosa gives **sensation**, not squeeze strength

answer: Disruption of the external anal sphincter (voluntary skeletal muscle)
why: A difficult delivery with a **third-degree tear** disrupts the **external anal sphincter**, the voluntary muscle supplied by the **pudendal nerve**. She loses **squeeze pressure**, so urgency and cough overcome continence.
chain: Rectal contents leak with urge or cough

idea.rule: A weak voluntary anal squeeze means damage to the external sphincter or its pudendal nerve supply.
also: Pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) stretch in prolonged labor
Cauda equina or sacral cord lesions
Sphincter division during anal fistula surgery

stem: A 38-year-old man eats a large meal, and vagal stimulation drives acid secretion by gastric parietal cells. This part of acid secretion is blunted by atropine but not by an H₂ blocker.
oneliner: 38M + meal + vagal drive to parietal cells + blocked by atropine, not by H₂ blocker → which messenger releases ER calcium?
ask: Which of the following intracellular messengers most directly releases calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum?

whyNot.A: Made by **Gs** receptors, as for histamine H₂
whyNot.C: Made through **guanylyl cyclase**, as with nitric oxide
whyNot.D: A **gas** that activates guanylyl cyclase, not a Gq second messenger
whyNot.E: A **membrane-derived mediator** of prostaglandins; it does not release ER calcium

answer: IP3 from PIP₂
why: ACh binds the **M3 receptor**, which activates **Gq and phospholipase C**. PLC cleaves **PIP₂ to IP3 and DAG**. **IP3 releases ER calcium**, which with DAG-activated PKC drives the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
chain: PLC cleaves PIP₂ into IP3 and DAG

idea.rule: Gq receptors signal through PIP₂-derived IP3 (calcium) and DAG (PKC).
also: α1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
H1 receptors in allergy
V1 receptors on vessels
Gastrin (CCK-B) on parietal and ECL cells

stem: A hormone is extracted from the mucosa of the duodenum and proximal jejunum and infused into an anesthetized dog. Pancreatic juice becomes rich in digestive enzymes with little extra bicarbonate. The gallbladder contracts and the sphincter of Oddi relaxes.
oneliner: Extract from duodenal and proximal jejunal mucosa infused in dog → enzyme-rich pancreatic juice, little bicarbonate + gallbladder contracts, sphincter of Oddi relaxes → which hormone?
ask: Which of the following hormones was most likely infused?

whyNot.B: Raises **bicarbonate-rich** juice, not enzyme-rich
whyNot.C: Raises **secretion and motility** of intestinal fluid, not enzyme-rich pancreatic juice
whyNot.D: Pancreatic islet hormone that **relaxes** smooth muscle
whyNot.E: Made in the **antrum**, stimulates acid secretion

answer: Cholecystokinin from duodenal I cells
why: **CCK** is made by **I cells** of the duodenum and proximal jejunum in response to fat and amino acids. It stimulates **enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion**, contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi.
chain: Fat and amino acids reach duodenum
Sphincter of Oddi relaxes; bile and enzymes flow

idea.rule: CCK (fat, protein) means enzymes and bile; secretin (acid) means bicarbonate.
also: CCK delays gastric emptying
CCK produces satiety
Fatty meal provokes biliary colic in gallstone disease
Sincalide (CCK analog) tests gallbladder emptying on HIDA scan

stem: A 5-month-old boy has chronic diarrhea, poor weight gain and edema with a low serum albumin. His pancreatic juice contains normal amounts of trypsinogen but almost no trypsin activity. Adding an extract of normal duodenal mucosa to the juice restores activity.
oneliner: 5-month-old boy + chronic diarrhea, poor weight gain, edema, low albumin + normal trypsinogen, no trypsin activity in juice + duodenal mucosal extract restores it → what is missing?
ask: Which of the following is most likely deficient?

whyNot.A: Acts in the **stomach** and is not needed to activate pancreatic trypsinogen
whyNot.B: An **active pancreatic enzyme** activated by trypsin, not an activator
whyNot.C: Another **pancreatic protease** activated by trypsin
whyNot.D: Stimulates **bicarbonate** release; it does not convert zymogens

answer: Enteropeptidase deficiency
why: **Enteropeptidase** (enterokinase) on the **duodenal brush border** cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates the other pancreatic zymogens. Without it, protein is poorly digested, giving **diarrhea, edema and failure to thrive**.
chain: Trypsinogen is not converted to trypsin

idea.rule: A single brush-border enzyme switches on the whole pancreatic protease cascade.
also: Trypsin activates chymotrypsinogen, proelastase and procarboxypeptidase
Trypsin activates prophospholipase A2 and procolipase
Trypsin activated inside the gland starts the cascade in acute pancreatitis

stem: A 28-year-old healthy man volunteers for a physiology study. Olive oil is instilled through a tube into his duodenum, and within minutes a hormone made by I cells of the duodenal mucosa rises in his blood.
oneliner: 28M volunteer + olive oil in duodenum + I-cell hormone rises → effect?
ask: Which effect is most directly produced by this hormone?

whyNot.A: CCK **slows gastric emptying**; it does not speed the stomach
whyNot.B: CCK drives **exocrine** pancreatic enzyme release, not endocrine hormones
whyNot.D: Not a CCK effect; fat in the gut does not cause **vasoconstriction**
whyNot.E: Acid output is raised by **gastrin from G cells**, not by this I-cell hormone

answer: Gallbladder contraction (cholecystokinin)
why: Fat in the duodenum triggers **I cells to release cholecystokinin**. CCK makes the **gallbladder contract** and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, delivering bile to emulsify the fat.
chain: Fat and amino acids reach the duodenum
Bile enters the duodenum to emulsify fat

idea.rule: Nutrients in the duodenum release the hormone that brings the secretion needed to digest them.
also: Acid in the duodenum releases secretin, which stimulates bicarbonate secretion
Fat and amino acids also make CCK stimulate pancreatic enzyme release
Glucose in the gut releases GIP, which enhances insulin release

stem: A 50-year-old man is having a cholecystectomy. Bile from his hepatic duct is compared with bile drawn from his gallbladder. The gallbladder sample is several times more concentrated in bile salts and bilirubin, though the total amounts of those solutes are the same in both.
oneliner: 50M + gallbladder bile far more concentrated in bile salts and bilirubin, same total solute → what leaves the bile?
ask: Which substance is absorbed by the gallbladder epithelium to produce this difference?

whyNot.A: Bilirubin is **concentrated**, so it stays in the bile rather than being absorbed
whyNot.B: Cholesterol is carried in micelles and **stays in the lumen**; absorbing it would not concentrate bile
whyNot.C: Calcium is a minor bile solute; its removal would not explain a **several-fold** concentration
whyNot.D: Lecithin forms mixed micelles with bile salts and **remains** in the bile

answer: Water (with Na+ and Cl-)
why: The gallbladder epithelium **actively absorbs Na+ and Cl-**, and **water follows**. Removing water while the solutes stay behind **concentrates bile** 5- to 20-fold.
chain: Gallbladder epithelium pumps out Na+ and Cl-
Bile salts, bilirubin and cholesterol are left concentrated

idea.rule: A storage organ concentrates its contents by absorbing solvent, not by adding solute.
also: Proximal tubule reabsorbs isotonic fluid; collecting duct concentrates urine with ADH
Colon absorbs water to form formed stool
Gallbladder concentration also raises the saturation of cholesterol, favoring stones

stem: A 66-year-old man has a colonic adenocarcinoma. Histology shows tumour cells that have broken through the epithelial basement membrane into the lamina propria.
oneliner: 66M + colon adenocarcinoma + tumour cells breach basement membrane into lamina propria → which activity allowed it?
ask: Activity of which of the following most directly allowed this step?

whyNot.B: An **adhesion** molecule; its **loss**, not its activity, lets cells detach
whyNot.C: Gives **unlimited replication**, not matrix breakdown
whyNot.D: Drives **angiogenesis**, not digestion of the basement membrane
whyNot.E: Drives **G1 to S** progression, not invasion

answer: Type IV collagenase (a matrix metalloproteinase)
why: The basement membrane is rich in **type IV collagen**. Invasive cells lose E-cadherin, then secrete **matrix metalloproteinases** (**type IV collagenase**) that digest it so they can enter the stroma.
chain: Type IV collagen of basement membrane is degraded
Path opens to vessels and metastasis

idea.rule: Invasion needs proteolytic digestion of the basement membrane and matrix.
also: Matrix metalloproteinases in most invasive carcinomas
Loss of E-cadherin favors detachment
Laminin receptors help tumor cells attach to the basement membrane
Cathepsins and urokinase assist breakdown

stem: A healthy 2-day-old term boy, feeding well, is noticed to be mildly yellow. The jaundice began after the first day. His hemoglobin and reticulocyte count are normal, and the raised bilirubin is almost entirely unconjugated. He is expected to be well and to turn normal color within two weeks.
oneliner: 2-day-old term boy + well + jaundice after 24 hours + normal Hb and reticulocytes + unconjugated bilirubin → which step is limited?
ask: Immaturity of which step of bilirubin handling most likely explains his jaundice?

options.C: Conjugation of bilirubin by glucuronyl transferase
options.D: Binding of bilirubin to plasma albumin
options.E: Excretion of conjugated bilirubin into bile

whyNot.A: Normal hemoglobin and reticulocytes argue against **excess hemolysis**
whyNot.B: The **enzyme**, not its glucuronic acid substrate, is immature in a healthy term newborn
whyNot.D: Albumin carries bilirubin in blood; poor binding raises the **free fraction**, not the total, and nothing here (drugs, prematurity) lowers it
whyNot.E: Impaired excretion would raise **conjugated** bilirubin, but his is almost all unconjugated

answer: Conjugation of bilirubin to glucuronic acid (immature UGT)
why: Newborn liver has **immature UDP-glucuronosyltransferase**, so conjugation of bilirubin to glucuronic acid is slow. This causes **unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia** after 24 hours, peaking at days 3 to 5, in an otherwise **healthy infant with normal hemoglobin**.
chain: Mild yellow skin from day 2, peaks day 3 to 5

idea.rule: Jaundice with normal hemoglobin in a well newborn means slow conjugation, not hemolysis.
also: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathologic until proven otherwise
Crigler-Najjar: absent or severely reduced UGT1A1
Gilbert syndrome: mildly reduced UGT1A1
Phototherapy converts bilirubin to water-soluble isomers

stem: A 55-year-old man has had 2 months of difficulty swallowing and regurgitation of undigested food. His breath smells bad and he hears rumbling in his neck. A swallowing study shows a 4-cm sac arising from the back wall of the lower pharynx in the midline, just above the upper esophageal sphincter.
oneliner: 55M + 2 months of dysphagia + regurgitation of undigested food + halitosis + neck rumbling + posterior midline sac just above the upper esophageal sphincter → which mechanism forms the sac?
ask: Which of the following best explains how this sac formed?

options.A: Traction from scarred mediastinal lymph nodes
options.B: Loss of myenteric inhibitory neurons in the lower esophagus
options.D: Poor cricopharyngeus relaxation raising pressure above it
options.E: Congenital outpouching of all wall layers

whyNot.A: Traction pulls out a **mid-esophageal** tent-shaped sac; this one is in the **lower pharynx above the upper sphincter**
whyNot.B: Affects the **lower esophagus**, but this sac lies **above the upper esophageal sphincter**
whyNot.C: A foregut septation defect shows up in the **newborn**; he is **55** and the problem began 2 months ago
whyNot.E: A congenital sac of all layers would not first cause symptoms at **age 55**; this one appeared in an **older man**

answer: Poor cricopharyngeus relaxation raising pressure above it
why: Failure of the **cricopharyngeus to relax** in step with swallowing raises **pressure in the hypopharynx**. Mucosa and submucosa bulge through the weak Killian triangle **above the muscle**, forming a false (pulsion) diverticulum that fills with food.
chain: Mucosa pushes through the weak Killian triangle above the muscle
A false pouch of mucosa and submucosa forms
Food collects: regurgitation, halitosis, neck gurgling

idea.rule: Pulsion diverticula are false pouches pushed out by high pressure; traction diverticula are true pouches pulled out by scar.
also: Traction diverticulum: mid-esophagus, from scarred lymph nodes (for example tuberculosis); a true diverticulum
Epiphrenic diverticulum: above the lower sphincter with a motility disorder; a pulsion pouch
Colonic diverticula: false pouches at weak points where vasa recta pierce the wall
Meckel diverticulum: a true congenital pouch containing all wall layers

stem: A 39-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and obesity has had 2 days of epigastric pain that goes through to her back, with vomiting. Blue-gray discoloration covers both flanks. Her blood draw looks milky, and small yellow papules are on her elbows and buttocks. She drinks no alcohol and had her gallbladder removed 3 years ago. Serum lipase is 10 times normal.
oneliner: 39F + poorly controlled diabetes and obesity + epigastric pain to the back + flank discoloration + milky blood + yellow papules + no alcohol, no gallbladder + lipase ×10 → which metabolic abnormality caused it?
ask: Which of the following metabolic abnormalities most likely caused her condition?

whyNot.A: Causes weakness and arrhythmia, not **milky blood** and **yellow papules**
whyNot.C: Causes gout and kidney stones; it does not make the blood **milky** or cause **yellow papules**
whyNot.D: Causes irritability of nerves and muscles; it does not explain **milky blood**
whyNot.E: Follows water loss and causes thirst and confusion; it does not explain **milky blood**

answer: High serum triglyceride level
why: **Milky (lipemic) blood and eruptive yellow xanthomas** in a woman with **poorly controlled diabetes**, with **no alcohol and no gallbladder**, point to severe hypertriglyceridemia. Triglycerides above about 1000 mg/dL release toxic free fatty acids in the gland and cause pancreatitis.
chain: Insulin deficiency and obesity raise VLDL and chylomicrons
Pancreatic lipase splits them into free fatty acids
Free fatty acids injure acinar cells and small vessels
Enzymes activate inside the gland: pancreatitis

idea.rule: Outside gallstones and alcohol, the main metabolic causes of acute pancreatitis are very high triglycerides and hypercalcemia.
also: Hypercalcemia from hyperparathyroidism activates trypsinogen
Eruptive xanthomas and lipemic serum mark severe hypertriglyceridemia
Estrogens, pregnancy and uncontrolled diabetes can push triglycerides above 1000 mg/dL
Familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency (type I) causes chylomicronemia and pancreatitis in childhood

stem: A 19-year-old man has had 3 days of worsening abdominal pain, and today he notices pain in his right shoulder. For 2 weeks he has taken ibuprofen several times daily for a wrist sprain and had burning upper abdominal pain. His temperature is 39 C. The abdomen is rigid with rebound tenderness. An upright chest x-ray shows a crescent of air under the right hemidiaphragm. The shoulder looks normal and moves painlessly.
oneliner: 19M + daily ibuprofen with burning epigastric pain + 3 days of worsening abdominal pain + new right shoulder pain + fever 39 C + rigid abdomen with rebound + air under the right hemidiaphragm + normal shoulder → which nerve carries the shoulder pain?
ask: The shoulder pain is carried by which of the following nerves?

whyNot.A: Carries visceral pain from foregut organs to the midline upper abdomen, not from the **diaphragm** under which the **air** collects
whyNot.B: Supply the outer rim of the diaphragm and chest wall; irritation there is felt over the **lower ribs**, not the **shoulder**
whyNot.C: Carries parasympathetic and visceral signals, not **shoulder skin** pain from **diaphragm** irritation
whyNot.D: Carries midgut visceral pain felt at the umbilicus, not at the **shoulder**

answer: Phrenic nerve (C3-C5)
why: **Air under the diaphragm** with **fever and peritonitis** after weeks of **ibuprofen** is a perforated peptic ulcer. Gas and fluid irritate the **central diaphragm**, supplied by the **phrenic nerve (C3-C5)**. The same cord segments receive shoulder skin, so the pain is felt at the shoulder.
chain: A perforated viscus spills gas and fluid under the diaphragm
Phrenic nerve afferents carry the signal to spinal cord segments C3-C5
Those segments also receive shoulder skin
The brain perceives the pain at the shoulder

idea.rule: Referred pain is felt in skin that shares a cord segment with the irritated structure.
also: Kehr sign: left shoulder pain from a ruptured spleen under the diaphragm
Gallbladder inflammation reaching the diaphragm: right shoulder or scapular pain
Early appendicitis: periumbilical pain through T10 visceral afferents
Myocardial infarction: pain to the left arm and jaw

stem: A 4-year-old boy has had 3 months of loose watery stools, a swollen belly and loud gurgling after meals. His stools are acidic with no blood or mucus. His growth is normal and he has never had surgery. Symptoms clear within a day of stopping milk, ice cream and cheese, and also stop when he fasts. The stool osmotic gap is 180 mOsm/kg. A hydrogen breath test after a milk drink shows a rise in breath hydrogen.
oneliner: 4M + 3 months of watery stools, distention, gurgling after meals + acidic stool without blood + normal growth + clears off dairy and with fasting + osmotic gap 180 + rise in breath hydrogen → which mechanism causes the diarrhea?
ask: Which of the following best explains his diarrhea?

options.A: Toxin-driven chloride secretion through raised cAMP
options.B: Immune-mediated villous damage triggered by gliadin
options.C: Mucosal inflammation causing bloody, leukocyte-rich stool
options.D: Bile acid loss from terminal ileal disease
options.E: Unabsorbed sugar drawing water into the bowel lumen

whyNot.A: Secretory diarrhea **continues with fasting** and has a low osmotic gap; his **stops with fasting** and his gap is **180**
whyNot.B: Would cause poor growth and not clear within a day of dairy avoidance; his **growth is normal**
whyNot.C: His stool has **no blood or mucus**, and symptoms follow **dairy**
whyNot.D: Needs ileal disease or resection; he has **never had surgery**, and symptoms follow **dairy**

answer: Unabsorbed sugar drawing water into the bowel lumen
why: Diarrhea that **stops with fasting and dairy avoidance**, with a **high osmotic gap**, **acidic stool** and **rising breath hydrogen**, is osmotic. Lactose that is not digested stays in the lumen and holds water; colonic bacteria ferment it to gas and acids.
chain: Brush-border lactase is low in the small intestine
Lactose is not split into glucose and galactose
Unabsorbed lactose raises luminal osmolality and holds water
Colonic bacteria ferment it to gas and short-chain acids
Watery acidic diarrhea, bloating, borborygmi and raised breath hydrogen

idea.rule: In osmotic diarrhea the stool osmotic gap is high and the diarrhea stops with fasting; in secretory diarrhea the gap is low and it continues.
also: Osmotic gap = 290 minus 2 times (stool Na plus K); above about 125 mOsm/kg is osmotic
Osmotic laxatives (lactulose, magnesium salts) work the same way
Secretory causes: cholera, ETEC, VIPoma
Celiac disease can cause secondary lactase deficiency
